chunks.section: Introduction Optomec is a new powerful tool for additive manufacturing
chunks.text: Introduction Optomec is a new powerful tool for additive manufacturing. It is changing the way materials are printed or adhered to substrates and/or features. The Optomec is an aerosol jet printer and will be my main focus on this project. It has the unique capabilities including a small minimum feature size (10 um) and it can apply a wide range of inks or materials with varying viscosities, for example from 1 cP to 1000 cP. This manual is a documentation that will accompany the user-friendly tutorial videos. These are guidelines that will explain how to use the Optomec effectively and suggest some of the novel things that one can achieve with them for projects in robotics, medical devices, etc. It can support research on a wide range of applications including device with resistors and transistors on flexible electronics. It can even support biological applications, where it can deposit live cells on a wide variety of substrates. It will be widely useful to future researchers in robotics, medical devices, bio-hybrid machines, etc. As an example application depositing PEdot on flexible PDMS substrates for electrostatic adhesion and sensing systems in robotics. Tutorial set up videos are ideal to help new users and non frequent users get up to speed on the tool. Please view all the videos and review this document before attending training. These videos show the step by step process on how to assemble, disassemble the machine, convert CAD models, and design layouts into the software which commands the machine to print. These online videos are available at all times so the user can review as many times as needed and has some prior knowledge before coming to the first training session. This manual will live next to the Optomec and will be used when the user is operating the machine. chunks.text: Aerosol-Jet Printed Fillets for Well-Formed Electrical Connections between Different Leveled Surfaces Abstract: As additive manufacture becomes more prevalent in the fabrication of advanced electronics, there is a need to create well-formed, robust circuitization, and interconnects between components mounted onto different leveled surfaces (DLSs). Here, an algorithm is developed for aerosol-jet printing of fillet structures that enable such a circuitization and hence a smooth electrical transition between the DLSs. The fillets are printed using an ultraviolet-curable polymer ink in the presence of in situ curing. A specific deposition rate is established in order to ensure a precise architecture. Further, a surface smoothing technique is employed to smooth out the stepped surface topology of a fillet resulting from the layer-by-layer printing of in situ cured material. Finally, it is ascertained that the performance of these printed fillets is highly satisfactory by carrying out the resistance measurements of the conducting lines printed over these fillet structures both before and after temperature cycling and establishing the mechanical stability of the fillets by employing an adhesion test. This technology ensures that the fillets not only establish a mechanical integration/attachment of the two DLSs, but more importantly that they also provide a well-formed surface onto which an electrical connection between these two DLSs can be established. 1. Introduction Additive manufacturing (AM) (also known as 3D digital printing technologies or more colloquially as 3D-printing) is a promising manufacturing method, which allows for the design and fabrication of complex structures not otherwise achievable using standard (subtractive) manufacturing methods. Additive manufacturing methods have been utilized extensively in the area of structural prototyping in, for example, the automotive and aviation industries. Further advances in AM are bringing the fabrication of electronics into the realm of 3D printing. Such additive manufacturing methods for the fabrication of electronics are expected to greatly advance the design of both printed hybrid electronics (PHE) and flexible hybrid electronics (FHE), which are predicated on the expectation that advanced electronic circuits will be constructed such that new form factors can be obtained. For the PHE this would be in the form of conformable/embedded electronics, while for FHE

For the PHE this would be in the form of conformable/embedded electronics, while for FHE this would be fully flexible electronics. For example, advanced electronics could provide, for some applications, an alternative to a standard Cu/FR4 flat, rigid printed circuit boards (PCBs) generally found in present-day computers and other electronics devices such that the electronics could be fabricated directly into the part itself. Examples of such advanced electronics are a smart electronic bandage for the health care industry or an impact sensor and/or communication electronics built into the shell of a sports helmet. Such electronics are expected to require the ability to mount and electrically connect components comprised of different materials and thicknesses (i.e., embedded/integrated components rather than surface-mounted components that were attached as the last step in fabrication) during the fabrication of a desired circuit. While the ability to thin the components in order to achieve true flexibility may be needed for FHE, PHE is expected to be able to utilize components of varying thicknesses. However, this will most likely require a robust way of creating a smooth transition onto and off of the embedded components, i.e., to smoothly route electrical interconnects over surfaces with inherent step transitions, that is to say between different leveled surfaces (DLSs), as alluded to in Figure 1. Furthermore, a capability is needed to precondition uneven or rough surfaces to a required smoothness value so that well-formed electrical circuits and interconnects can be deposited. In order to address these essential requirements, in this study we have developed algorithms for designing smooth transitions between surfaces and have developed robust processing methods for the fabrication of these transition ramps that are designed to smoothly connect (both electrically and mechanically) DLSs. Typically, smooth transitions between DLSs (combination of a bare IC chip and a substrate is a typical example of a DLSs system) are achieved by syringe-dispensing an epoxy or underfill type

Typically, smooth transitions between DLSs (combination of a bare IC chip and a substrate is a typical example of a DLSs system) are achieved by syringe-dispensing an epoxy or underfill type material around the edge of a component in a way that is illustrated in Figure 1b. While this may be adequate for large-scale features and low densities of thick interconnects, as is reported by Seifert et al., a more controllable method is expected to be required as feature sizes and thicknesses are reduced and interconnect densities are increased. As advanced circuits become smaller and more complex, a more precise control over the volume of the material deposited and the exact geometry of a printed fillet (the structure used to smooth out the height transitions between surfaces) is needed. Therefore, we have developed an aerosol-jet (AJ) printing method for the precise control of the geometry of a printed fillet for the creation of a smooth structural transition between DLSs. The unique printing algorithm consists of (a) a precise determination and regulation of the deposition rate of a printed polymer ink, which is in situ cured and (b) the employment of a novel smoothing and gap-filling approach by printing the same polymer ink followed, after an appropriate time delay, by a postprinting cure. Most importantly, we establish that our printing strategy ensures continuous 3D printed conductive circuits across DLSs, with the circuits demonstrating robust thermal stability and good adhesion properties. The most important feature of the fillet technology that we have developed is that rather than the fillets being a by-product of the mechanical attachment of an object to a surface, they are a precisely engineered and fabricated structure to support an electrical conductor transitioning between DLSs. Our fillet technology is distinctly different from the fillets present in all the current wire-bonded chip packages used in industries. In these chip packages, the fillets are merely used to mechanically integrate the two DLSs, while the electrical connection between these two surfaces is achieved

chunks.text: electrical conductor transitioning between DLSs. Our fillet technology is distinctly different from the fillets present in all the current wire-bonded chip packages used in industries. In these chip packages, the fillets are merely used to mechanically integrate the two DLSs, while the electrical connection between these two surfaces is achieved via wire bonding. Our study provides a completely alternative mechanism for electrically connecting DLSs by using fine-pitch printed conductors over microstructured fillets. This approach has important advantages over wire-bonding, such as (a) not requiring the extra space in the z-direction and the longitudinal direction that is required to accommodate the arch of the bond-wire, (b) not requiring clearance between adjacent pads to accommodate the wire-bond tool capillary, (c) eliminating the risk of short-circuits between adjacent conductors, where bond wires have increasing risk of short-circuits as interconnect density increases, (d) reducing the electrical length of interconnect, and (e) limiting and controlling the electrical impedance discontinuity caused by the interconnect. In all, we believe that our proposed fillet technology is a significant advance of the current state-of-the-art in the broad area of fabrication and integration. 2. Modeling of Fillets In much the same way that other 3D printing methods slice up the volume of a structural part so that it can be printed one layer at a time, a surface transition ramp (termed a fillet in this paper) can also be sliced. In general, the slicing is performed perpendicular to the ink stream so that uniform layers can be deposited. Figure 2 illustrates two interesting orientations for which a surface transition ramp might be sliced. The ability to print such surface fillets is dependent on the geometry attainable with a given tool platform. For example, the fillet illustrated in Figure 2a would require a printing system equipped with a vertically mounted (z-axis direction) print-head and only an x-y stage as illustrated in Figure 3a, while the fillet illustrated in Figure 2b would further require either the print-head or the part to be rotated by 45° as illustrated in Figure 3b. Additionally, for the orientation shown in Figure 2b, the part (or print-head)

Depending on the part and/or the tool platform size, there may not be enough room within the printer to accommodate such an orientation. While the 45° orientation might be more desirable, on a two or three-axis tool platform it could require refixturing the part multiple times to reach all the desired part orientations. In general, however, it would require a five-axis tool platform to implement. While five-axis tool platforms are expected to become more available, currently many printers are not equipped with the ability to easily tilt a part or print-head. Therefore, we will focus on developing methods for printing ramps using tool platforms restricted to motion along only three orthogonal directions. This restriction will require a part orientation as shown in Figure 3a and a slicing geometry as shown in Figure 2a. The width of an ink stream is much narrower than the dimensions of the fillet layers, as illustrated in Figure 2a, so each slice/layer will need to consist of a serpentine fill. If, for the purpose of creating a toolpath, the cross-sectional area of the first single printed line can be modeled using a triangular shape of height (h) and base (2h), then each layer can be segmented into serpentine lines on a pitch (p) equal to the height (h) of the modeled triangle of this first printed line as illustrated in Figure 4. Setting the pitch of the serpentine lines to be equal to the height of this modeled triangle ensures a good overlap between printed lines in a given layer, which can help in the formation of a smooth, continuous layer surface. Further note that the closest approach of the center of the ink stream to the vertical sidewall is equal to one-half of the ink stream width (w). This restriction is to ensure that extra material does not build up on the top surface during printing. This restriction is illustrated in Figure 4 and results in only half the needed material being printed at the sidewall. This deficiency was overcome by adding an extra line at the sidewall for each layer printed with half as much material (by printing at twice the linear print speed, as discussed later). Design requirements related to this restriction will be presented in more detail following the main development of the algorithm for creating a printed fillet. The overall dimensions of a fillet and the dimensions for a single area element (equal in area to the cross-sectional area of a single printed line) are illustrated in Figure 4. The cross-sectional area of the fillet (A) can be expressed as A = H²/2. The volume of the fillet (V) is given as V = Al = (H²/2)l. And the cross-sectional area of a single area element (a) is given as a = h². In the above equations, H is the distance between the DLSs and h is the height of a single area element. Of course, Equations (1)–(3) assume that both the entire fillet as well as the single area element can be modeled as isosceles right triangles. Now, the total number of printed lines (N) needed to create a fillet is simply the number of area elements that are needed to fill the fillet cross sectional area. Therefore N = A/a = H²/(2h²). Furthermore, the number of total slices/layers (n) needed to create the fillet is by definition n = H/h. For a fillet of length (l), the total length (L) of all the printed lines added together is given as L = Nl = (H²/2h²)l. As with the printing of any layer or feature(s), the total print time (T) can be obtained as the ratio of the total volume to be printed (V) to the deposition rate (R) of material volume per unit time or the ratio of the total length to be printed (L) to linear print speed (s). So, T = L/s = V/R. This can be rewritten as R/S = V/L = Al/Nl = a. Employing these equations to design and then print a fillet will result in a structure similar to that illustrated in Figure 4. Given that the ink stream cannot be centered at the vertical transition between DLSs, only half the desired material will be deposited at the sidewall, thus creating a "gap." To account for this "gap," an extra line of material at the sidewall can be printed at a speed of 2s after the completion of the printing of each layer. If this extra material has a low-enough viscosity and is not immediately cured, this deposited material, due to the favorable self-wettability and the resulting surface tension forces at the sidewall, will be able to flow into the gap and fill it. In reality, not all the extra uncured material flows into the gap, but rather some sticks to the previously printed line. Additionally, once a fillet has been fully printed, a seam can exist between the top surface of the DLSs and the top of the fillet; therefore, it is good practice to also print an extra line to seal this seam and provide a smooth transition at the top of the fillet. Furthermore, "bulb" formations, as discussed by others, may happen at the termination of a printed feature due to build plate decelerations and time delays related to shutter opening and closing. In order to minimize effects related to such "bulb" formation, the ends of a fillet were tapered inward as illustrated in the inset of Figure 4. An additional issue related to the AJ printing of a fillet is expected to be related to the viscosity of the ink. In order to be able to aerosolize a material for printing, the viscosity will have to be in a range where the ink, once printed onto a surface, will flow and therefore not retain a desired shape. For a UV-curable polymer ink, however, this can be overcome by curing the material in situ. However, such in situ processing tends to produce topologies that result in nonflat surfaces because the material is not allowed to flow enough to self-level. In the printing of fillets, this effect will tend to produce a stair-step type structure as one layer is printed on top of another, as illustrated in the inset of Figure 4 and in Figure 5. The resulting fillet surface can be smoothed by printing an additional layer of material that is allowed to flow and self-level prior to curing. While compelling capabilities have been demonstrated in the research community in recent years, the development and refinement of inks and process parameters largely follows empirical observations, with an extensive phase space over which to optimize. While this has led to general qualitative guidelines and ink- and machine-specific correlations, a more fundamental understanding based on principles of aerosol physics and fluid mechanics is lacking. This contrasts with more mature printing technologies, for which foundational physical principles have been rigorously examined. Presented here is a broad framework for describing the AJP process. Simple analytical models are employed to ensure generality and accessibility of the results, while experimental validation using a silver nanoparticle ink supports the physical relevance of the approach. This basic understanding enables a description of process limitations grounded in fundamental principles, as well as guidelines for improved printer design, ink formulation, and print parameter optimization. chunks.text: aerosol gas flow ratio Printed electronics is an emerging application area for functional nanomaterials, with widespread utility spanning flexible circuits and displays, electronics packaging, and environmental and biomedical sensing. In a typical process flow, liquid inks containing dispersed nanomaterials are deposited with high pre-cision using a suite of printing methods, such as inkjet, aerosol jet, gravure, flexographic, and screen printing. While many of these techniques have an exten-ded history, aerosol jet printing (AJP) is a relatively recent addition to the printing toolbox. In AJP, a functional ink is aerosolized and delivered to the sub-strate by a carrier gas, achieving resolution as fine as 10 µm. Due to its non-contact, line-of-sight, and digi-tal nature, AJP offers advantages complementary to many traditional methods. AJP has been employed in academic research for slightly over a decade in a wide variety of demonstrations. Some of the first examples of use include transistors and more complex circuits, and it continues to be widely used in this field today. More recently, microscale additive man-ufacturing was demonstrated by AJP, in which three-dimensional scaffold structures with hierarchical por-osity were demonstrated using a silver nanoparticle ink. AJP has been used in applied areas of research, for example metallization of photovoltaics and circuit boards, as well as newer fields such as perovskite and kesterite solar cells and terahertz metamaterials. A hallmark of AJP, and a fea-ture underlying its expanding use, is its versatility and compatibility with a broad range of materials, from organic semiconductors and carbon nanomaterials to functional ceramics and composites. Despite its prevalent use in academic research, AJP has several drawbacks well-known to day-to-day users. Although the process is tolerant of a wide range of inks, determining optimal print parameters is often a sensitive process. Related to this, consistency and reproducibility are challenging to achieve, and can require extreme measures such as frequent replace-ment of ink, hindering translation to a production environment. Finally, optimal printing parameters for a given ink do not in general translate to new materials, demanding an extensive, empirical optimization over a broad phase space for each additional ink or mat-erial. These problems stem, in large part, from a lim-ited fundamental understanding of the process. While mature methods such as inkjet and gravure printing have been widely studied for decades, and have a body of knowledge describing the underlying physical mechanisms, the nascent technique of AJP cannot leverage such a strong theoretical foundation. In the rare attempts to address this need, analyses have largely focused on a single aspect of the overall process. This work is an effort to remedy that shortcoming. Basic models for the discrete physical processes involved in AJP are assembled to develop a more comprehensive understanding of the overall method. Simple, analytical models are deliberately chosen over more involved numerical simulations to maintain generality and accessibility, and to more effectively intuit and conceptualize the underlying physics. Despite the rudimentary nature of the mod-els, some of which represent textbook scenarios in aerosol physics and fluid mechanics, the resulting description is well validated by experiments. This pro-vides a valuable benchmark for experimental results, to identify and correct inefficiencies in the ink chem-istry and process conditions. Moreover, this basic understanding of the principles of AJP enables an exploration of process limitations grounded in funda-mental fluid mechanics, providing guidelines for improved printer design, ink formulation, and print parameter optimization. Results and discussion AJP overview A general schematic of AJP, broken down into its component physical processes, is shown in figure 1(a). Ultrasonic atomization is used to generate droplets of the active ink. Due to the micron-scale size of the droplets, solvent evaporation occurs rapidly, resulting in a reduction in droplet size. A carrier gas, referred to herein as the aerosol gas, transports the droplets to the deposition head. During transit, two mechanisms can lead to losses—gravitational settling and impingement on tube walls by diffusion. In the deposition head, a sheath gas surrounds the aerosol gas, collimating the beam. As they pass through a deposition nozzle, droplets can be diverted from their flow stream due to inertial effects in the narrow, converging nozzle, leading to aerodynamic focusing. Finally, the droplets are directed towards the substrate in an impinging jet. Each of these processes can be described with knowl-edge of the system geometry and the key process parameters—the aerosol and sheath gas flow rates, the deposition nozzle size, and the aerosol droplet size. Additional parameters such as atomizer power, print speed, and ink and substrate temperatures are con-trolled in operation, but have peripheral effects around the core processes. Atomizer power and ink temper-ature (which affects viscosity) affect the inputs to the process, namely droplet size distribution and aerosol density. While atomizer power and ink temperature are not explicitly treated here, the droplet size distribu-tion and aerosol density are considered. In addition, print speed affects the print thickness and the substrate temperature affects

While important for the process, deviations due to these effects are largely ink-specific. Therefore, this work will address these factors as they fold in around the core AJP process, without an explicit treatment. There are two primary commercial systems for AJP. The most prevalent one, having been around for over a decade, is manufactured by Optomec. The experimental portion of this work employs an alternative design from Integrated Deposition Solu-tions, Inc. known as the Nanojet (figure 1(b)). Due to its simple design, this machine is amenable to the broad study of process parameters included here. While constructed differently, these printers operate on the same general mechanism described above, and can provide an informative contrast when assessing the principles of the process. Therefore, general principles will apply to both systems, while specific results dependent on system geometry will consider the Nanojet geometry, with comparisons drawn in cases for which the printer design has a strong impact on operation. In the same way, the experimental portion of this work will employ a silver nanoparticle ink due to its practical relevance, but the basic physical principles and models can be applied to diverse inks, including particle-free formulations. High frequency (MHz) ultrasound sets up a capillary wave on the ink surface, leading droplets to break off with a fairly well defined size distribution. The ink viscosity and amount determine the critical power required for atomization, as the ultrasonic wave must propagate through the liquid to the surface with limited viscous damping. The droplet size generated is related to the capillary wavelength, determined by the ultra-sound frequency, the ink density, and the ink surface tension. Based on the expected median number diameter for droplets and a log-normal distribution to model polydispersity, figure 1(c) shows idealized diameter distributions (weighted by droplet number and mass) for xylene and water, representing two inks with widely varying surface tension. Due to their micron-scale sizes, aerosol gas droplets quickly lose solvent upon contact with a dry gas stream. The resulting reduction in drop size facilitates uptake in the aerosol carrier gas stream, which is expected to become saturated with solvent vapor on a timescale of seconds under typical operating condi-tions. As a result, the droplet size is largely stable dur-ing transport from the cartridge to the deposition head, until coming into contact with the sheath gas. To prevent complete drying of aerosol droplets, it is com-mon practice to design inks with ~10% of a low-vola-tility cosolvent. This helps maintain generality of results here, droplet size will be explicitly controlled as a vari-able, and in most cases considered as a distribution. Processes that vary considerably with droplet size, then, will be strongly coupled with the ink formulation. Moreover, droplet size polydispersity will be exacerbated by dry-ing effects. Because the droplet size distribution is an important parameter for the various physical pro-cesses downstream, more detailed, process-specific modeling of aerosol evaporation will be addressed in guide ink design in future work. A more qualitative discussion is included here to preserve generality of the results while still considering the important effects coupling the droplet size with physical processes and experimental outputs. Aerosol transport Following atomization, the aerosol gas carries ink droplets through the mist tube to the deposition head. During this process, which can take on the order of 10s under typical operating conditions, droplets colliding with the walls are lost. Material impinging on the walls is not printed, leading to changes in the deposition rate. Moreover, as this material builds up over time, it can lead to process drift, contaminate or even clog the deposition head, and overall limit the printing lifetime. Two physical mechanisms are con-sidered here for transport losses: gravitational settling and diffusion. Broadly speaking, large droplets are more susceptible to gravitational settling, while small droplets exhibit increased diffusion, defining a win-dow of droplet sizes useful for processing. In addition to droplet size, the gas flow rate and geometry of the mist tube are key parameters. Gravitational settling is treated based on the work of Thomas. The survival probability, or fraction of droplets remaining suspended, is a function of the geometry, droplet size, and flow rate, as described by equation (1). Figure 2(a) shows the survival probability as a function of droplet size for various flow rates, based on an approximate geometry for the Nanojet system. This effect functions as a soft, low-pass filter on droplet size, and can be controlled during operation by selection of the flow rate. Intuitively, larger droplets require a high flow rate to be carried through the mist tube without settling, and even at high flow rates an appreciable fraction of aerosol droplets are lost. In practice, the survival probability can be integrated over a distribution of droplet sizes to account for polydispersity. Aerodynamic focusing Aerodynamic lensing offers an opportunity to colli-mate the aerosol beam beyond the volume displace-ment focusing effect of the sheath gas. As the aerosol beam travels through the narrow, converging nozzle, the inertia of droplets can cause them to deviate from the gas flow streamlines. In a well-constructed aerodynamic lens, droplets can be shifted towards the flow centerline. This effect is sensitive to the droplet size and the geometry of the lens, and is widely exploited in aerosol mass spectrometry and other analytical techniques. It is common to describe effects of inertial forces using the dimensionless Stokes number, shown in equation (3). For a conventional thin-plate orifice, optimal focusing occurs for a Stokes number (St) near 1. Smaller droplets have less inertia, and therefore follow the flow streamlines more closely, leading to ineffective focusing. Larger droplets are more dramatically diverted from their initial flow streamlines, leading to over-focusing for Stokes number greater than ~2 in a typical geometry. Impaction Following ejection from the deposition nozzle, the aerosol droplets travel towards the substrate in an impinging jet. Qualitatively, small droplets, or those without enough inertia, are carried by the flow streamlines away from the axis of deposition. The smallest droplets do not impact the surface at all, as in a traditional inertial impactor, while droplets approaching a critical size will impact but with a broadened deposition pattern. Here this is treated following Flagan and Seinfeld based on cylind-rical stagnation flow. Figure 5(a) shows calculated droplet trajectories for a range of droplet sizes, with blue indicating 'populated' trajectories and red indicating 'vacant' trajectories arising from the sheath gas. The sheath gas increases the jet velocity, leading to higher droplet inertia, and pushes the aerosol droplets onto more central streamlines, where spreading is mini-mized. Small droplets exhibit a broad distribution pattern, a hallmark of AJP commonly referred to as overspray. The focusing efficiency describing broad-ening of the impaction pattern is a function of droplet size, nozzle diameter, and flow rates. This focusing efficiency is plotted against droplet size in figure 5(b) for constant flow rates (10/100 sccm aerosol/sheath gas flow) and several different nozzle diameters. Each curve asymptotes at the cutoff for impaction, and droplets approaching this cutoff yield a more diffuse impaction pattern. A sharper cutoff at lower diameter is calculated for the smaller diameter nozzles, due to increased flow velocity and inertia of the droplets. A distribution of droplet sizes is considered in figure 5(c), which shows the calculated line profile for different median droplet diameters. This further shows the effect of droplet size, and results in a line profile characteristic of AJP with a dense core region surrounded by diffuse overspray. Nonidealities While the mechanisms discussed thus far are relevant for proper AJP, several sources of nonideality are briefly mentioned here. First, rapid deposition of a wet ink leads to excessive fluidity on the substrate, which can lead to increased line spreading or fluid instabil-ities. In practice, this can be mitigated by increasing the printing speed and reducing the deposition rate. Deposition of a moderately dry ink can lead to an enhanced resolution, as the sheath gas dries droplets around the periphery of the aerosol stream. Once substantially dried, these droplets can fall below the critical Stokes number for impaction. Due to the micron-scale nature of the droplets, under common operating conditions in a wide-bore geometry the increase in vapor concentra-tion due to evaporation can largely offset the loss due to diffusion, leading to a sharp drying front moving radially inward. Conclusion The analysis of AJP undertaken here offers a general and accessible framework for understanding and improving the technology. By exploring several key physical processes involved in printing, complex interactions between printer design, ink formulation, and print parameter selection are revealed. Aerosol losses during transport from the cartridge to the deposition head can be considered, with effects on the deposition rate and, in some cases, the consistency over an extended print. The focusing effect of the sheath gas is described analytically based on simple volume displacement, leading to a simple relation describing a baseline resolution estimate as a function of the nozzle diameter and focusing ratio. In addition, cases for which additional aerodynamic focusing effects are expected are considered. Impaction effects can also be understood from basic models, resulting in a more refined window of process parameters for efficient printing. Moreover, with this general frame-work in place, nonidealities and deviations related to flow, pressure, and ink design can be identified and understood. Although this approach employs simple models, key experiments validate its physical rele-vance, and the relative simplicity allows relationships to be understood on an intuitive, conceptual level. Moreover, this approach identifies physical processes that are particularly important and complex, thus meriting more sophisticated modeling. For example, the droplet size distribution is important for transport, focusing, and impaction, and is a dynamic variable dependent on the ink formulation and process parameters. Furthermore, effective aerodynamic len-sing is likely to be important for pushing the limits of resolution, and numerical modeling of the specific deposition nozzle geometry would be valuable in this regard. While it is grounded in basic, analytical descriptions of key physical processes, this approach offers a strong foundation for better understanding the interrelationships between parameters and pro-cesses. Moreover, the mathematical framework pro-vides an opportunity for issues of process sensitivity and reliability to be explored. Overall, this adds a valuable component to the AJP toolbox, and marks a step towards a greater fundamental understanding characteristic of more mature printing methods.

chunks.text: The Optomec Aerosol Jet HD2 Motion and Vision Manual with KEWB provides detailed information about the system's operation, maintenance, and safety procedures, with a focus on its motion and vision capabilities. **Chapter 1: AJ System Description** **1.1 Safety Precautions** To prevent personal injury, improper operation, or system failure, it is crucial to observe safety precautions. Safety stickers are placed on the system, as detailed in document 9001016 AJ 5X, FLEX, 200, and HD2 Safety Sticker Placement. * **All systems - Deposition material:** Consult appropriate safety data sheets (SDS) for proper handling of all inks, pastes, and other materials used in the AJ system. * **Inhalation danger:** The AJ system can produce atomized particles of material that are easily inhaled. Use proper protection and ventilation when using the system. * **Gas pressure:** Adhere to the pressure ratings specified for gases introduced into the AJ system. Over-pressurizing the system can result in improper operation, system failure, or personal injury. * **Electrical shock:** The AJ HD2 system has a power distribution panel. Danger! Do not open this panel without first terminating the source power. Failure to comply with this warning may result in serious personal injury. * **Motion stages:** The high-speed movements of the AJ HD2 motion stages can cause injury. Keep arms and fingers away from the system during the deposition process. * **Optional heaters - Burn danger:** If the AJ system has a heated platen, use caution. The heated platen can reach temperatures of 120°C (248°F), causing severe burns. * **Optional UV cure module - High intensity ultraviolet light hazard:** If your system includes the UV cure module, review safety precautions and operating instructions in the user manual. Safety precautions include mandatory use of ultraviolet-blocking protective goggles or a face shield, and recommended use of long-sleeved shirts or lab coats, and ultraviolet-opaque gloves to protect hands. * **Optional laser modules - Invisible laser radiation (laser sintering tool):** Danger: Laser radiation when open and interlock defeated. Avoid eye or skin exposure to direct or scattered radiation. * **Invisible laser radiation – laser distance sensor:** Caution: Laser radiation when open and interlock defeated.

The Z-axis has 100 mm of travel, sitting on the X-axis which has 420 mm of travel (120 mm used for moving between the print head and other payload tools). The Y-axis has 300 mm of travel and moves the 300 x 300 mm heated vacuum chuck for part holding and heating. An optional 4th axis (R, Rotation about Z-axis) is available for indexing or orienting part surfaces for printing on vertical sidewalls and into trench geometries using optional fixed tilt brackets. The motion system uses direct drive linear and ball-screw stages with high-precision glass scale encoders for optimal positioning. It achieves static bi-directional positional accuracy of +/-5 µm in XY and +/- 12 µm in Z, and static bi-directional repeatability of +/- 2 µm in XY and +/- 6 µm in Z (within a 25 mm cubic volume within the full 300x300x100 mm travel). Rails are mounted directly to the granite substructure, enabling clean printing motion at accelerations up to 1.5 G without losing print fidelity. **1.13 Vision System** The vision system typically comprises an alignment camera and a process viewing camera. The process camera is an optional feature. **1.13.1 Alignment Camera** The Digital Alignment Camera aligns the deposition head to the substrate. Its viewing window is on the upper monitor. The alignment vision system has a 44 mm working distance, resolving objects as small as 4 µm, allowing it to view SMEMA-standard fiducials. An optional fine resolution setup with 18 mm working distance resolves objects as small as 2 µm. This high-resolution video lens and imager produce quality images for pattern matching or feature detection. The image from the alignment camera is viewable via the KEWB Live Vertical Feed button. **1.13.2 Process Viewing Camera** The Digital Process Viewing Camera views the deposition area, displaying its window on the lower monitor. During operation, the image is continuously viewable via the KEWB Live Process Feed button. **Chapter 2: KEWB** **2.1 KEWB Overview** The Aerosol Jet® Printer is a high-precision 3-axis machine featuring the HD2™ print head, capable of printing fine-feature patterns (as small as 10µm) onto almost any surface, with positional accuracies of +/-5 µm in XY and +/- 12 µm in Z. The KEWB software offers a user interface for developing sequences or manually operating the system. The sequencer allows engineers to design specific steps to automate operations, creating repeatable processes that utilize the system's full functionality. Each sequence step performs a unary task specific to a functional area, enabling easy reproduction of printed products. The main screen lets engineers or operators monitor process devices (pressure controls, heaters/chillers, etc.). The alarms tab displays system alarms that disable the system in unwanted situations. The help screen includes a PDF viewer for the Aerosol Jet Printer Manual. The engineer screen provides full system functionality to qualified engineers, while the user screen supports multiple users for security. The vision screen allows loading new COG jobs for tasks like alignment correction. **2.2 Important Terms** * **Alarm:** An abnormal machine condition, configurable by the user or hard-coded. * **Inspection:** A vision program that captures an image from a camera and processes it using tools to produce results, usually indicating part presence or position. * **Recipe:** A sequence of instructions for running ink in the system, typically provided by Optomec. Any variable expression can be monitored against custom values or ranges. A background poller continuously checks and reports alarms. When triggered, an alarm can display a message, pause/abort motion, or run embedded commands. The poller and enabled alarms from the last exit start automatically on program startup. Note: The poller status "Last Update" time continuously updates when the poller is active. The alarm configuration interface uses a spreadsheet-like format. Each row (1) represents an alarm, with cells containing user-defined properties. Menus (2) offer options to add new alarms, restart an inactive poller, and define system variable options. The bottom (3) shows the poller's current status, including the last update time. Some alarms are read-only (XML editable) and have a red background. When an alarm's conditions are met, it triggers and appears on the Alarms Screen, requiring acknowledgment. Additional actions may occur. While triggered, the poller does not evaluate it. After acknowledgment, it re-enables, and polling resumes. **3.4.1 Alarm Properties and Components** Each alarm has properties and components; invalid fields show a red exclamation point. * **Enabled:** Check to activate the alarm, continuously monitoring trigger conditions. If not, the poller has stopped and should be restarted. **3.4.4 Using Alarms** 1. Create a new alarm via Menu Options. 2. Assign a descriptive name. 3. Set expressions for variables or constants in the "bound 1," "variable," and "bound 2" fields. Available variables are on the Variables Screen. Invalid expressions will show a red error icon and prevent enabling. 4. Select appropriate comparisons for fields. If no comparison operator is specified, no evaluation occurs. If an adjacent field is blank, no evaluation occurs even if an operator is set. * **Example 1 (single constant bound):** Exhaust pressure (VI_EXH_MFC_Pressure) must not drop below -2. It accommodates board sizes from 70-290 mm length/width and up to 25 mm height, with max weight 4 pounds. Workpieces should not have protruding components on the underside. The conveyor has a SMEMA interface for upstream/downstream communication. An upstream machine signals readiness to send a board, which the HD2 accepts when ready. The HD2 then signals readiness to send the board to the downstream machine, and sends it when accepted. **7.1.1 Gripper and XZ actuators** The gripper picks up boards and places them on the heated vacuum platen. Its fingers adjust to board width and act as guide rails. The gripper is attached to XZ actuators, allowing boards to be moved. **7.1.2 Roller sections** Two roller sections accept boards from upstream and send them downstream. A board fully inside the HD2 contacts the board end stop, squaring up with gripper rails for alignment. **7.1.3 Laser shutter doors** Shutter doors protect users from laser beams and help contain printed materials. They open/close for board passage and have spring-loaded safety mechanisms. Interlocks ensure doors are closed during normal operation; they trigger an alarm and prevent laser firing if open. **7.2 Homing** **7.2.1 Gripper and XZ actuators** XZ actuators have limit sensors for homing and preventing travel beyond allowable space. Homing is done via the "Home" button in the conveyor user interface. The "Homing Required" indicator shows if homing is needed. **7.3 Running your first board** **7.3.1 Setup** 1. Place the HD2 in-line with upstream and downstream machines. Ensure machines are leveled and conveyor sections align. The front edge of the board should align 1.8” from the front edge of the roller section. 2. Determine conveyor direction by changing the `xml key` value (`true` or `false`) in `Process_Configuration.xml` (located in `C:\AerosolJetPrinter\Config`). 3. chunks.text: Aerosol Jet™ Health and Safety Guidelines The purpose of this document is to outline health and safety guidelines for the safe handling and disposal of nanoparticles utilized or generated during the use of Aerosol Jet deposition technology. 1 Electrical Safety Do not operate the ultrasonic atomizer (or produce aerosol) without a material vial installed. Avoid contact with the water or ink spout generated by the ultrasonic atomizer. 2 Chemical Safety The ASTM Committee on Nanotechnology has defined a nanoparticle as a particle with lengths in two or three dimensions between 1 and 100 nanometers (nm). Nanoparticles can be composed of many different base materials and may be of different shapes including: nanotubes; nanowires; and crystalline structures such as fullerenes and quantum dots. Nanoparticles present a unique challenge from an occupational health perspective as there is a limited amount of toxicological data currently available for review. However, some studies have shown that existing exposure control technologies have been effective in reducing exposure to nanoparticles. As such, the accepted exposure control hierarchy was utilized in the development of this document. Types of chemicals used in the Aerosol Jet process: The types of chemicals used in the Aerosol Jet process include: Acids (cleaning), Bases (surface modification), Organic solvents, Powders and nano-materials, Organometallic precursors, Miscellaneous materials (polymers, solder pastes, flux, adhesives, etc.), and Aerosols containing the materials listed above. Risks The primary routes of exposure for nanoparticles are inhalation, dermal absorption, and ingestion. Nanoparticles or nanomaterials used in laboratory experiments will likely be in one of three forms: a powder, in suspension, or in a solid matrix. The form of the nanoparticles or nanomaterial will play a large role in the exposure potential. For example, a nanoparticle in powdered form will present a larger inhalation hazard potential than a nanoparticle in suspension. Some common tasks that present some potential for exposure include: * Working with nanoparticles in suspension without gloves; * Working with nanoparticles in suspension during pouring or mixing where agitation is involved; * Generating nanoparticles in the gas-phase; * Handling nanoparticle powders; * Maintenance on equipment used to produce nanoparticles; * Cleaning

The concentration of hazardous aerosols inside the enclosure may take significant time to decay to a safe level after deposition is halted. This decay time depends on the deposition process and materials. Users should measure the exposure levels for their specific operation. Always carefully read the material MSDS information prior to loading, printing, and unloading material (ink) into the aerosol jet system. OSHA Table Z-1 at: https://www.osha.gov/pls/oshaweb/owadisp.show document?p_table=standards&p_id=9992 4 Pressure Safety Under typical conditions, the Aerosol Jet apparatus operates at pressures ranging from approximately 1 to 10 psi. The gas source however may be pressurized to several thousand psi. Care should be taken to avoid over-pressurizing the system. All portable gas sources should be secured. 5 Mechanical Safety The Aerosol Jet System has both automatic and manual motion control stages that are capable of high-speed operations that can injure personnel. Keep arms and fingers away from the system during the deposition process. All motion can be stopped by depressing the emergency stop bottom on the emergency override panel. 6 Disclaimer The data contained in this Health and Safety section is believed to be true and accurate, but is offered solely for your consideration, investigation, and verification. Our systems meet U.S. OSHA safety threshold levels for an 8-hour TWA; however, there are concerns about exposure before this time period. Optomec would like to caution its customers to consult the MSDS for each material they use in either system to ensure that safety recommendations are followed. Aerosol Jet Etching (AJE) – Efficiencies of laboratory-fabricated silicon solar cells (25%)1,2 significantly exceed those of typical commercial screen-printed cells (16-18%). – Need to replace photolithographic dielectric patterning processes (used by the high efficiency laboratory cells) with cheaper processes. – Photolithographic patterning of dielectric layers involves patterning of a resist layer followed by immersion etching. – When compared with immersion etching processes, AJE offers: • Fewer steps; • Uses small amounts of inexpensive chemicals and produces less hazardous F waste; and • Safer than existing immersion etching processes in that HF is only formed locally where etching is required. chunks.text: • What are your most common aerosol jet printing inks? • Our standard conductive ink is Novacentrix Metalon JS-A426 and can be printed straight from the bottle without dilution, our standard insulating/dielectric ink is a 2:1 ratio of acetone and Norland NEA 121 which is a common, commercially available electronics adhesive • What is the viscosity range compatible with aerosol jet printing? • For ultrasonic atomization, target inks in the range of 1-10 cP (water-blood), for pneumatic atomization, aim for 1-100cp (water-oil) • What temperature is needed to cure/sinter silver ink? • You can sinter silver ink in at 100°C for 12 hours, 185° C for 4 hours, 250 deg. C for 10 minutes. Ensure that the sintering conditions will not damage the substrate or other circuit components that will exposed to the same heat, choose a lower temperature and longer time if you are unsure about the thermal limits of your system • What are some common solvents used in aerosol jet print ink formulation? • Deionized water, acetone, isopropanol (IPA), toluene, propylene glycol methyl ether acetate (PGMEA), N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), and terpineol are all common solvents used in aerosol jet printing. It is important to match the added solvent to the existing ink solvent system for compatibility. • What is the ideal standoff distance for an aerosol jet printing nozzle? • The ideal standoff distance is between 3 and 7mm, this distance is set by the calibration procedure within the “Set Z-height with Alignment Camera to Nozzle offset” sequence. Ensure that the nozzle will not collide with taller components on the substrate at the chosen offset distance • How do I shrink/expand my ink spot size? • To decrease your feature size, increase the sheath gas flow rate (S_MFC) to further focus the ink stream, to increase your feature size, decrease your sheath gas flow (S_MFC) • How do I increase my ink deposition rate? • Increasing the atomizer energy (UA_MAX) or increasing your atomizer flow rate (ATM_MFC) will increase your ink deposition rate • How can I speed up drying of my ink once it is printed? •

If the print is looking dry or discontinuous, continue to add more passes by running the toolpath again to build up material • What print and rapid speeds should I be operating the printer? • It is recommended to print at 2-3mm/s and use a rapid speed of 10 mm/s (which is the speed that the printer jogs between features). It should be noted that print speed also influences your deposition rate, the slower you move • How long will my ink stay stable and useable in the printer’s ink vial? • Aerosol jet printer inks are solvent based and will begin evaporating as soon as they are formulated, they are usually stable as long as solvent is being added back in the printing process but will dry out and become unprintable if the ink is left unattended. The printer should be cleaned at the end of each print session and new ink should be loaded the next time the printer is used • What solvent should I use in the solvent addback system? • The solvent in the add-back system should match the solvent base for the ink being printed, for example, use deionized water for Novacentrix Metalon JS-A426 silver ink and acetone for Norland NEA 121 dielectric ink • How should I store aerosol jet print inks when not in use in the printer? • Follow manufacturer recommendations for

Inks like Novacentrix Metalon JS-A426 are meant to be stored in a refrigerator at less than 5°C and inks like Norland NEA 121 should be stored in amber or opaque vials since it is UV-curable. • Is it possible to remove a printed trace once it has been printed? • Printed traces are liquid until they are cured/sintered so they can often be wiped away with the appropriate solvent and a lint-free swab. The longer the trace sits on the substrate the harder it will be to remove. Be sure to clean the area thoroughly before attempting to reprint the trace. • What happens if I hit a mechanical limit switch in the course of operating the printer? • Hitting a limit switch will pause all motion and throw an alarm within the KEWB software. Navigate to the “Alarms” button on the bottom right of window, click “Ack All Alarms” as many times as necessary to clear the flashing red alarm codes and then manually jog the printer back into the safe zone (move up in the “z” direction first and then towards the center of the platen using the “x” and “y” jog buttons • What happens if I fail my initial leak check? • Failing a leak check could be indicative of a few issues but will require you to remove the printer cartridge to diagnose. First, check all o-rings in the ink vial assembly to assure they are properly seated and not damaged, replace any o-rings that appear dry, cracked, discolored or caked in ink material. Next ensure that the cartridge is well-seated against the printer alignment pins and that latch is secured, finally check the tube connections between the ink tube, vial assembly and nozzle to ensure they are well sealed. Attempt another leak check once the printer is reassembled. • Can I print multiple ink materials on top of one another? • This is possible, but you must fully cure each printed layer before adding another material. Silver inks should be sintered with the laser sintering module or at the appropriate time and temperatures and dielectric inks should be heat cured or UV cured to ensure successive layers do not blead into one another. • What should I do with the printer once the session is complete? • Stop all process conditions using the “Shutdown UA Process” sequence, wait until the printer registers as “idle” and then disassemble. Clean all ink-contaminated components in a beaker of the base solvent, placing the beaker in a sonicator to ensure a deep clean. The longer the ink sits in the system the more likely it is to corrode internal components so clean promptly after each print session.
